extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy; instructors and scholars of Plato
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of an excerpt from Plato's Republic (Book X) discussing the nature and civic role of poetry, the soul's principles, and the myth of Er about choices after death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic imitation as inferior to truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitative poet's creations have an inferior degree of truth; he is a manufacturer of images and is very far removed from the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates compares the imitative poet to the painter: both produce likenesses that are not the true things but images. This inferiority in truth is a central objection to admitting imitative poetry into a well-ordered State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry appeals to the irrational part of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is concerned with an inferior part of the soul and prefers the passionate and fitful temper, which is easily imitated, rather than the rational principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because imitative art targets emotions (pity, laughter, lust, anger) it aims at the irrational elements in people, not the reasoned, self-governing part. That makes it ill-suited for education in virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude imitative poets from the well-ordered State
rubrics_metrics.description: We shall be right in refusing to admit the imitative poet into a well-ordered State, because he awakens and nourishes and strengthens the feelings and impairs the reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: as a city where the evil rule and the good are put aside is corrupted, so the soul is corrupted when imitative poetry empowers irrational passions. Admission into the State is judged by the work's effect on reason and moral constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry can harm even the good by stimulating passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry feeds and waters the passions (pity, laughter, lust, anger) instead of drying them up; it lets them rule when they ought to be controlled if mankind are to increase in happiness and virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: noble listeners delight in pity at tragic recitation but would condemn such behaviour in themselves during real misfortune; comic jests make people laugh at unseemly things they'd be ashamed to do. These effects show poetry's potential harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable poetic content: hymns and praises
rubrics_metrics.description: Hymns to the gods and praises of famous men are the only poetry which ought to be admitted into our State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates allows a narrow class of poetry: works that praise the gods or honour esteemed persons. Other forms (epic, lyric that stimulate pleasure/pain) are excluded because they risk making pleasure and pain the rulers instead of law and reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry must prove usefulness to State and human life
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry's defenders must show not only that it is pleasant but also that it is useful to States and to human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates permits defenders of poetry to speak in verse or prose to demonstrate usefulness; if the defence fails, poetry must be given up despite its charms. Usefulness to civic education and moral life is the critical test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art and temperament should follow reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The higher principle (reason) is ready to follow the suggestion of law: to be patient under suffering, take counsel, and apply remedies rather than indulge in lamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This normative ideal contrasts the rational handling of hardship with the irrational principle's tendency to recollect troubles. Arts (including poetry) should reinforce the higher principle by modeling reasoned responses, not uncontrolled lamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the life which makes the soul more just
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting a life (in the myth of Er), one should choose the life which will make his soul more just and give the name of evil to the life which will make his soul more unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The myth of Er's lottery of lives instructs that choices must be evaluated by their effect on the soul's justice: consider how wealth, birth, beauty, strength, cleverness, and station combine with soul qualities to determine whether a life is good or bad for moral character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue is free and the chooser bears responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is free, and as a man honours or dishonours her he will have more or less of her; the responsibility is with the chooser—God is justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the selection of lives, moral responsibility lies with the chooser: one cannot blame fate alone. This functions as a normative rule about moral agency and accountability when evaluating life-paths or actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know how to choose the mean and avoid extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: One should know how to choose the mean and avoid the extremes on either side, as far as possible; this is the way of happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical evaluation: when choosing among alternative lives or actions, weigh the combined effects on virtue and aim for moderation rather than extremes. The passage advises using discriminating knowledge to discern the better life.
